items.stem: Which of the following best describes "endemic species"?
options: A limit on the mass of fish that can be caught, to keep fish stocks sustainable
Protecting species in their natural habitat, e.g. national parks
A measure of biodiversity that combines richness and evenness: D = 1 − Σ(n/N)²
A species found naturally in only one geographic area
items.answer: A species found naturally in only one geographic area
items.markingKey: D. "endemic species" is a species found naturally in only one geographic area.

items.stem: Briefly explain why species richness alone can give a misleading picture of biodiversity.
items.answer: Two habitats can have the same number of species but one may be dominated by a single species; evenness must also be considered.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Two habitats can have the same number of species but one may be dominated by a single species; evenness must also be considered. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A field of one crop with millions of plants has high biodiversity." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: A monoculture has very low biodiversity: one species dominates and few others are present.
items.markingKey: A monoculture has very low biodiversity: one species dominates and few others are present. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Kenji wants to find out how the distance downstream from a sewage outlet affects the biodiversity of freshwater invertebrates. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does distance downstream from the outlet affect simpson’s diversity index of invertebrates?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (distance downstream from the outlet (0, 50, 100, 200, 400 m)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (Simpson’s diversity index of invertebrates from a 1-minute kick sample) in a question form.

items.stem: Briefly describe Kick sampling for the Biological Monitoring Working Party (BMWP) score and explain what it reveals about measuring biodiversity in practice.
items.answer: Freshwater invertebrates are sampled by kicking the stream bed into a net; each family scores points for its pollution sensitivity and the total indicates water quality. It is a cheap, standardised method used by environmental agencies to monitor rivers.
items.markingKey: Context (Freshwater invertebrates are sampled by kicking the stream bed into a net; each family scores points for its pollution sensitivity and the total indicates water quality.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It is a cheap, standardised method used by environmental agencies to monitor rivers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to measuring biodiversity in practice.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the distance downstream from a sewage outlet affects the biodiversity of freshwater invertebrates. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): wear waders and gloves; check depth and flow; cover cuts (risk of Weil’s disease); work in groups. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. wear waders and gloves; check depth and flow; cover cuts (risk of Weil’s disease); work in groups); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: A stream contains many mayfly and stonefly larvae. What does this suggest?
options: The water is clean and well-oxygenated
items.answer: The water is clean and well-oxygenated
items.markingKey: B. They are indicator species.

items.stem: Define the term "species evenness".
items.answer: How evenly the individuals are distributed among the species present
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: how evenly the individuals are distributed among the species present. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between species evenness and species richness.
items.answer: Richness is how many species are present; evenness is how equal the numbers of each species are.
items.markingKey: Richness is how many species are present; evenness is how equal the numbers of each species are. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between species evenness and species richness.
items.answer: Richness is how many species are present; evenness is how equal the numbers of each species are.
items.markingKey: Richness is how many species are present; evenness is how equal the numbers of each species are. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A quadrat survey found: daisy 30, clover 5, dandelion 5. Calculate Simpson’s diversity index using D = 1 − Σ(n/N)².

Jonas counted the number of lichen species on tree trunks at different distances from a city centre (three trees at each distance).

Distance from city centre / km | Lichen species per tree: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 3 | 3 | 3
3 | 6 | 6 | 6
5 | 8 | 8 | 8
8 | 12 | 12 | 12
12 | 17 | 17 | 18

Calculate the mean lichen species per tree when the distance from city centre was 3 km.
items.markingKey: M1 (6 + 6 + 6) ÷ 3; A1 6.0 (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Kick sampling for the Biological Monitoring Working Party (BMWP) score shows measuring biodiversity in practice.
items.answer: Freshwater invertebrates are sampled by kicking the stream bed into a net; each family scores points for its pollution sensitivity and the total indicates water quality. It is a cheap, standardised method used by environmental agencies to monitor rivers.
items.markingKey: Context (Freshwater invertebrates are sampled by kicking the stream bed into a net; each family scores points for its pollution sensitivity and the total indicates water quality.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It is a cheap, standardised method used by environmental agencies to monitor rivers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to measuring biodiversity in practice.

items.stem: Felix writes: "A field of one crop with millions of plants has high biodiversity." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A monoculture has very low biodiversity: one species dominates and few others are present.
items.markingKey: A monoculture has very low biodiversity: one species dominates and few others are present. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe how you would compare the biodiversity of a mown school lawn and an unmown meadow, and explain how you would process the data.
items.answer: Lay out grids; use random coordinates; place 10 × 0.25 m² quadrats in each habitat; identify and count each species (or % cover) using a key; calculate species richness and Simpson’s index D = 1 − Σ(n/N)² for each habitat; compare; repeat on different days; expect the meadow to have higher diversity because mowing removes tall species and allows a few grasses to dominate.
items.markingKey: Lay out grids; use random coordinates; place 10 × 0.25 m² quadrats in each habitat; identify and count each species (or % cover) using a key; calculate species richness and Simpson’s index D = 1 − Σ(n/N)² for each habitat; compare; repeat on different days; expect the meadow to have higher diversity because mowing removes tall species and allows a few grasses to dominate.

items.stem: Which wavelengths of radiation do greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit?
items.answer: Infrared
items.markingKey: A. Earth emits infrared.

items.stem: Explain how deforestation can reduce biodiversity beyond the area cut down.
items.answer: Remaining forest is fragmented into small patches that cannot support large animals; edges dry out; soil erodes into rivers; local rainfall decreases.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Remaining forest is fragmented into small patches that cannot support large animals; edges dry out; soil erodes into rivers; local rainfall decreases. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A cold winter proves global warming is not happening." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Climate is a long-term average; individual cold events do not change the global upward trend.
items.markingKey: Climate is a long-term average; individual cold events do not change the global upward trend. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Amazon deforestation and the tipping point and explain what it reveals about deforestation and climate.
items.answer: Since 1970 about 17% of the Amazon rainforest has been lost; scientists warn that at 20–25% loss parts could turn into savanna as rainfall decreases. Losing the Amazon would release huge amounts of carbon and destroy a major biodiversity hotspot.
items.markingKey: Context (Since 1970 about 17% of the Amazon rainforest has been lost; scientists warn that at 20–25% loss parts could turn into savanna as rainfall decreases.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Losing the Amazon would release huge amounts of carbon and destroy a major biodiversity hotspot. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to deforestation and climate.

items.stem: A pesticide is present in water at 5e-05 ppm. Its concentration increases 20× in plankton, 10× from plankton to small fish, and 15× from small fish to birds. Calculate the concentration in the birds and name this process.
items.answer: 0.15 ppm; biomagnification
items.markingKey: M1 5e-05 × 20 × 10 × 15; A1 0.15 ppm; B1 biomagnification (bioaccumulation along the food chain).

items.stem:
Zara predicts the outcome of an investigation into how the concentration of carbon dioxide in a sealed bottle affects the temperature rise when it is illuminated by a lamp.
(a) Formulate a hypothesis that includes a scientific explanation. [2]
(b) Identify the independent and dependent variables. [2]
(c) State two variables that must be controlled. [1]
(d) Sketch the shape of the graph you would expect if the hypothesis is correct and explain how it would support the hypothesis. [1]
items.answer: (a) If the CO₂ concentration is higher, then the temperature will rise more, because CO₂ absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation, modelling the greenhouse effect. (b) IV: percentage of CO₂ in the bottle (air ≈ 0.04%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%); DV: temperature rise in 15 minutes measured with a digital thermometer. (c) position of thermometer (shaded); distance from lamp and lamp power. (d) A graph of the DV against the IV showing the predicted trend; if the data follow this trend within the spread of repeats, the hypothesis is supported.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 testable prediction; 1 scientific reasoning: If the CO₂ concentration is higher, then the temperature will rise more, because CO₂ absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation, modelling the greenhouse effect. (b) 1 IV: percentage of CO₂ in the bottle (air ≈ 0.04%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%); 1 DV: temperature rise in 15 minutes measured with a digital thermometer. (c) 1 any two of distance from lamp and lamp power (affects energy received); size and colour of bottle (affects absorption); starting temperature (affects heat loss); position of thermometer (shaded) (direct light on the probe gives false readings). (d) 1 graph shape consistent with the hypothesis, linked to support.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the concentration of carbon dioxide in a sealed bottle affects the temperature rise when it is illuminated by a lamp. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Fill identical clear bottles with air or CO₂ mixtures (from a cylinder or reaction of acid and carbonate measured with a gas syringe); seal with a thermometer probe through the lid, shaded from direct light; place 30 cm from a 100 W infrared lamp; record temperature every minute for 15 min; repeat three times; plot rise against % CO₂.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (infrared lamps get very hot; CO₂ in high concentration can cause drowsiness – ventilate the room). Model: Fill identical clear bottles with air or CO₂ mixtures (from a cylinder or reaction of acid and carbonate measured with a gas syringe); seal with a thermometer probe through the lid, shaded from direct light; place 30 cm from a 100 W infrared lamp; record temperature every minute for 15 min; repeat three times; plot rise against % CO₂.

items.stem: Explain how the enhanced greenhouse effect leads to global warming and evaluate the evidence that humans are responsible.
items.answer: Sun’s short-wave radiation passes through atmosphere; Earth emits infrared; CO₂, methane and water vapour absorb and re-emit infrared, warming lower atmosphere; burning fossil fuels and deforestation raised CO₂ from 280 to over 420 ppm. Evidence: Keeling curve, ice-core CO₂–temperature correlation, isotopic signature of fossil carbon, warming pattern (stratosphere cooling), models only match with human emissions. Correlation alone is not causation, but multiple independent lines agree – strong scientific consensus.
items.markingKey: Sun’s short-wave radiation passes through atmosphere; Earth emits infrared; CO₂, methane and water vapour absorb and re-emit infrared, warming lower atmosphere; burning fossil fuels and deforestation raised CO₂ from 280 to over 420 ppm. Evidence: Keeling curve, ice-core CO₂–temperature correlation, isotopic signature of fossil carbon, warming pattern (stratosphere cooling), models only match with human emissions. Correlation alone is not causation, but multiple independent lines agree – strong scientific consensus.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "climate change"?
options: A species whose presence or absence shows the level of pollution or environmental quality
The number of different species in an area
Long-term changes in temperature and weather patterns, now largely caused by human activities
The protection and careful management of species, habitats and natural resources
items.answer: Long-term changes in temperature and weather patterns, now largely caused by human activities
items.markingKey: C. "climate change" is long-term changes in temperature and weather patterns, now largely caused by human activities.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The increased warming caused by extra greenhouse gases from human activities"?
items.answer: enhanced greenhouse effect
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of enhanced greenhouse effect.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the greenhouse effect and ozone depletion.
items.answer: The greenhouse effect involves gases trapping infrared and warming Earth; ozone depletion is the thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer by CFCs, letting more UV reach the surface.
items.markingKey: The greenhouse effect involves gases trapping infrared and warming Earth; ozone depletion is the thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer by CFCs, letting more UV reach the surface. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Global warming is caused by the hole in the ozone layer." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They are separate problems; global warming is caused by greenhouse gases trapping infrared, not by extra UV through the ozone hole.
items.markingKey: They are separate problems; global warming is caused by greenhouse gases trapping infrared, not by extra UV through the ozone hole. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between climate and weather.
items.answer: Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere; climate is the average weather over 30 years or more.
items.markingKey: Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere; climate is the average weather over 30 years or more. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the greenhouse effect is essential for life but the enhanced greenhouse effect is a problem.
items.answer: Without natural greenhouse gases Earth would average about −18 °C; extra gases from human activity trap more infrared, raising temperatures and disrupting climate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Without natural greenhouse gases Earth would average about −18 °C; extra gases from human activity trap more infrared, raising temperatures and disrupting climate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Mohammed used global data to compare atmospheric CO₂ concentration with average global temperature anomaly in different years (three data sets).

CO₂ concentration / ppm | Temperature anomaly / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
320 | 0.21 | 0.22 | 0.21
340 | 0.42 | 0.42 | 0.42
360 | 0.43 | 0.65 | 0.61
390 | 0.92 | 0.93 | 0.94
420 | 1.30 | 1.28 | 1.24

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean temperature anomaly at 360 ppm, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 0.43 °C (trial 1 at 360 ppm); mean = 0.63 °C
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (0.43) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 0.63 °C.

items.stem: A forest of 40000 km² loses 3000 km² per year. Calculate the percentage lost after 8 years at this rate.

Noah plans to investigate how the concentration of carbon dioxide in a sealed bottle affects the temperature rise when it is illuminated by a lamp. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: distance from lamp and lamp power; size and colour of bottle; starting temperature; position of thermometer (shaded)
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: distance from lamp and lamp power – affects energy received; size and colour of bottle – affects absorption; starting temperature – affects heat loss; position of thermometer (shaded) – direct light on the probe gives false readings. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Richer countries should pay poorer countries to protect their rainforests."
items.answer: Payment schemes are fair and useful if transparent and supporting local communities.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rainforests benefit the whole world (carbon, biodiversity); richer countries caused most historic emissions. Arguments against: payments may not reach local people or prevent illegal logging; sovereignty concerns. Supported judgement: Payment schemes are fair and useful if transparent and supporting local communities.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the concentration of carbon dioxide in a sealed bottle affects the temperature rise when it is illuminated by a lamp. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): infrared lamps get very hot; CO₂ in high concentration can cause drowsiness – ventilate the room. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. infrared lamps get very hot; CO₂ in high concentration can cause drowsiness – ventilate the room); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: "Individual actions, such as eating less meat, can make a real difference to climate change." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Individual actions help and influence others, but large-scale policy change is essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: food is about a quarter of emissions; diets matter; collective action shifts markets. Arguments against: energy, industry and policy changes have far larger effects. Supported judgement: Individual actions help and influence others, but large-scale policy change is essential. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Why are wildlife corridors created between habitats?
items.answer: They allow animals to move between fragments, maintaining gene flow
items.markingKey: They allow animals to move between fragments, maintaining gene flow. Reduces inbreeding.

items.stem: Zara writes: "Zoos are the best way to save endangered species." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Zoos help, but protecting wild habitats is usually more effective and keeps species’ natural behaviours and interactions.
items.markingKey: Zoos help, but protecting wild habitats is usually more effective and keeps species’ natural behaviours and interactions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between conservation and preservation.
items.answer: Conservation allows sustainable use of resources with management; preservation aims to keep areas untouched by humans.
items.markingKey: Conservation allows sustainable use of resources with management; preservation aims to keep areas untouched by humans. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to Grey wolves reintroduced to Yellowstone (1995), explain how it illustrates trophic cascades and rewilding.
items.answer: Wolves reduced elk overgrazing, allowing willows and aspen to recover, which helped beavers, songbirds and river banks. Top predators can restore whole ecosystems.
items.markingKey: Context (Wolves reduced elk overgrazing, allowing willows and aspen to recover, which helped beavers, songbirds and river banks.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Top predators can restore whole ecosystems. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to trophic cascades and rewilding.

items.stem:

items.markingKey: M1 means 23.0 and 104.0; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 +352.2% (increase).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Rewilding large areas of farmland in Europe would be beneficial."
items.answer: Rewilding less productive land can be very beneficial if planned with local communities.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: increases biodiversity and carbon storage; reduces flooding, tourism income. Arguments against: reduces food production; conflicts with farmers over predators such as wolves. Supported judgement: Rewilding less productive land can be very beneficial if planned with local communities.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "in situ conservation"?
options: Long-term changes in temperature and weather patterns, now largely caused by human activities
Protecting species outside their habitat, e.g. zoos, seed banks
Protecting species in their natural habitat, e.g. national parks
The trapping of infrared radiation emitted by Earth’s surface by gases in the atmosphere, keeping Earth warm
items.answer: Protecting species in their natural habitat, e.g. national parks
items.markingKey: C. "in situ conservation" is protecting species in their natural habitat, e.g. national parks.

items.stem: Briefly explain why fishing quotas are difficult to enforce.
items.answer: Oceans are vast and shared; illegal fishing and discarding of unwanted catch are hard to monitor; quotas may be set too high for political reasons.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Oceans are vast and shared; illegal fishing and discarding of unwanted catch are hard to monitor; quotas may be set too high for political reasons. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Saving one charismatic species, like the panda, saves the ecosystem." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Protecting panda habitat also protects many species (umbrella species), but whole ecosystems need wider management.
items.markingKey: Protecting panda habitat also protects many species (umbrella species), but whole ecosystems need wider management. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why seed banks are important for food security.
items.answer: They store genetic diversity of crops and wild relatives, which can be used to breed varieties resistant to new diseases or climate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They store genetic diversity of crops and wild relatives, which can be used to breed varieties resistant to new diseases or climate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Zara wants to find out how the mesh size of a fishing net affects the proportion of juvenile fish caught, using a model with different-sized beads. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does mesh size of the model net affect percentage of small “juvenile” beads?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (mesh size of the model net (5, 10, 15, 20 mm)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (percentage of small “juvenile” beads (8 mm) among the beads retained) in a question form.

items.stem: Ecologists caught and marked 60 fish in a pond and released them. A week later they caught 40 fish, of which 10 were marked. Estimate the population size (N = number marked × number in second sample ÷ number recaptured).
items.answer: 240 fish
items.markingKey: M1 60 × 40 ÷ 10; A1 240; (assumes marks not lost, no births/deaths/migration, random mixing).

items.stem: A rare orchid survives only in one small nature reserve. Evaluate three conservation strategies that could be used to protect it.
items.answer: In situ protection (fencing, managing grazing, controlling invasive species) – keeps natural pollinators but vulnerable to one disaster. Seed banking/tissue culture (ex situ) – insurance against extinction, preserves genetic diversity, but plants may lose adaptation. Creating new populations in suitable habitats/corridors – spreads risk, increases gene flow but needs suitable sites and pollinators. Best: combination, with monitoring and public education.
items.markingKey: In situ protection (fencing, managing grazing, controlling invasive species) – keeps natural pollinators but vulnerable to one disaster. Seed banking/tissue culture (ex situ) – insurance against extinction, preserves genetic diversity, but plants may lose adaptation. Creating new populations in suitable habitats/corridors – spreads risk, increases gene flow but needs suitable sites and pollinators. Best: combination, with monitoring and public education.

items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Define the term "deforestation".
items.answer: The large-scale clearing of forests, often for farming, logging or building
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the large-scale clearing of forests, often for farming, logging or building. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.answer: indicator species

items.stem: What is the purpose of captive breeding programmes?
options: To increase numbers of endangered species for possible release
items.answer: To increase numbers of endangered species for possible release

items.stem: Distinguish between the greenhouse effect and ozone depletion.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a habitat with high biodiversity is usually more stable.
items.answer: Many species and complex food webs mean that if one species declines, others can fill its role; populations are less likely to crash.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many species and complex food webs mean that if one species declines, others can fill its role; populations are less likely to crash. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between ex situ conservation and in situ conservation.
items.answer: In situ protects species in their natural habitats with all their ecological interactions; ex situ protects them outside, in zoos or seed banks, useful when habitats are destroyed.
items.markingKey: In situ protects species in their natural habitats with all their ecological interactions; ex situ protects them outside, in zoos or seed banks, useful when habitats are destroyed. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why plastic pollution harms marine food chains.
items.answer: Animals eat or are tangled in plastic; microplastics are eaten by plankton and pass up food chains, carrying toxic chemicals that accumulate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Animals eat or are tangled in plastic; microplastics are eaten by plankton and pass up food chains, carrying toxic chemicals that accumulate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: A monoculture has very low biodiversity: one species dominates and few others are present.
items.markingKey: A monoculture has very low biodiversity: one species dominates and few others are present. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why small, isolated populations are at greater risk of extinction.
items.answer: Low genetic diversity means fewer alleles to adapt to disease or change; inbreeding increases harmful recessive conditions; random events can wipe them out.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Low genetic diversity means fewer alleles to adapt to disease or change; inbreeding increases harmful recessive conditions; random events can wipe them out. State the CO₂ concentration at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 390 ppm; range = 0.04 °C; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 390 ppm; 1 range = max − min = 0.88 − 0.84 = 0.04 °C; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: A quadrat survey found: daisy 6, clover 6, dandelion 6, buttercup 6, plantain 6. Calculate Simpson’s diversity index using D = 1 − Σ(n/N)².
Using Grey wolves reintroduced to Yellowstone (1995) as an example, explain trophic cascades and rewilding.
items.answer: Wolves reduced elk overgrazing, allowing willows and aspen to recover, which helped beavers, songbirds and river banks. Top predators can restore whole ecosystems.
items.markingKey: Context (Wolves reduced elk overgrazing, allowing willows and aspen to recover, which helped beavers, songbirds and river banks.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Top predators can restore whole ecosystems. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to trophic cascades and rewilding.

items.stem: With reference to Amazon deforestation and the tipping point, explain how it illustrates deforestation and climate.
items.answer: Since 1970 about 17% of the Amazon rainforest has been lost; scientists warn that at 20–25% loss parts could turn into savanna as rainfall decreases. Losing the Amazon would release huge amounts of carbon and destroy a major biodiversity hotspot.
items.markingKey: Context (Since 1970 about 17% of the Amazon rainforest has been lost; scientists warn that at 20–25% loss parts could turn into savanna as rainfall decreases.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Losing the Amazon would release huge amounts of carbon and destroy a major biodiversity hotspot. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to deforestation and climate.

items.stem:
Noah counted the number of lichen species on tree trunks at different distances from a city centre (three trees at each distance).

Distance from city centre / km | Lichen species per tree: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 3 | 3 | 3
3 | 5 | 5 | 5
5 | 7 | 7 | 7
8 | 11 | 10 | 11
12 | 15 | 15 | 14

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The number of lichen species increases with distance from the city centre. Many lichens are sensitive to air pollutants such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are most concentrated near the city centre.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The number of lichen species increases with distance from the city centre.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Many lichens are sensitive to air pollutants such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which are most concentrated near the city centre.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the mesh size of a fishing net affects the proportion of juvenile fish caught, using a model with different-sized beads, state the dependent variable and describe how Lars should measure it.
items.answer: percentage of small “juvenile” beads (8 mm) among the beads retained
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: percentage of small “juvenile” beads (8 mm) among the beads retained.

items.stem:
Arjun used global data to compare atmospheric CO₂ concentration with average global temperature anomaly in different years (three data sets).

CO₂ concentration / ppm | Temperature anomaly / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
320 | 0.19 | 0.20 | 0.20
340 | 0.40 | 0.40 | 0.39
360 | 0.59 | 0.58 | 0.58
390 | 0.85 | 0.90 | 0.86
420 | 1.16 | 1.16 | 1.17

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The global temperature anomaly increases as CO₂ concentration increases – a positive correlation. CO₂ is a greenhouse gas that absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation from Earth’s surface; more CO₂ enhances the greenhouse effect. Correlation alone does not prove causation, but physics and other evidence support a causal link.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The global temperature anomaly increases as CO₂ concentration increases – a positive correlation.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: CO₂ is a greenhouse gas that absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation from Earth’s surface; more CO₂ enhances the greenhouse effect. Correlation alone does not prove causation, but physics and other evidence support a causal link.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Biodiversity should be protected mainly because of its value to humans (e.g. medicines, food)."
items.answer: Economic arguments help, but biodiversity is also worth protecting for its own sake and for unknown future value.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: provides medicines (e.g. aspirin from willow), food crops, pollination worth billions; easier to persuade governments. Arguments against: species have intrinsic value regardless of usefulness; we cannot predict which species will be useful. Supported judgement: Economic arguments help, but biodiversity is also worth protecting for its own sake and for unknown future value.

items.stem: "Marine protected areas where all fishing is banned are the best way to restore fish stocks." Discuss.
items.answer: No-take zones are highly effective when well enforced and combined with support for fishing communities.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fish populations and size increase rapidly inside reserves; spillover benefits nearby fisheries. Arguments against: loss of income for local fishing communities; hard to enforce over large areas. Supported judgement: No-take zones are highly effective when well enforced and combined with support for fishing communities. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Maya investigated how the concentration of carbon dioxide in a sealed bottle affects the temperature rise when it is illuminated by a lamp. The method had this weakness: the probe was in direct light so measured the probe heating, not the gas. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: shade the probe tip with a small foil cover
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: shade the probe tip with a small foil cover

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the distance downstream from a sewage outlet affects the biodiversity of freshwater invertebrates. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: At each distance, choose a riffle of similar depth; kick the stream bed upstream of a net for 1 min; empty into a white tray; identify and count invertebrates with a key; return them; calculate Simpson’s index; repeat three samples at each site; measure dissolved oxygen.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (wear waders and gloves; check depth and flow; cover cuts (risk of Weil’s disease); work in groups). Model: At each distance, choose a riffle of similar depth; kick the stream bed upstream of a net for 1 min; empty into a white tray; identify and count invertebrates with a key; return them; calculate Simpson’s index; repeat three samples at each site; measure dissolved oxygen.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A powerful greenhouse gas released by cattle, rice paddies, landfill and leaking gas wells"?
items.answer: methane
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of methane.

items.stem: Which ecosystem type has the highest species richness on land?
items.answer: Tropical rainforest
items.markingKey: B. Warm, wet, stable, many niches.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The protection and careful management of species, habitats and natural resources"?
items.answer: conservation
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of conservation.

items.stem: Leila writes: "Global warming is caused by the hole in the ozone layer." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They are separate problems; global warming is caused by greenhouse gases trapping infrared, not by extra UV through the ozone hole.
items.markingKey: They are separate problems; global warming is caused by greenhouse gases trapping infrared, not by extra UV through the ozone hole. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why lichens are used to monitor air pollution.
items.answer: Many lichen species are sensitive to sulfur dioxide; the number and type of lichens present indicate the air quality.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many lichen species are sensitive to sulfur dioxide; the number and type of lichens present indicate the air quality. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between preservation and conservation.
items.answer: Conservation allows sustainable use of resources with management; preservation aims to keep areas untouched by humans.
items.markingKey: Conservation allows sustainable use of resources with management; preservation aims to keep areas untouched by humans. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between ozone depletion and the greenhouse effect.
items.answer: The greenhouse effect involves gases trapping infrared and warming Earth; ozone depletion is the thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer by CFCs, letting more UV reach the surface.
items.markingKey: The greenhouse effect involves gases trapping infrared and warming Earth; ozone depletion is the thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer by CFCs, letting more UV reach the surface. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between species richness and species evenness.
items.answer: Richness is how many species are present; evenness is how equal the numbers of each species are.
items.markingKey: Richness is how many species are present; evenness is how equal the numbers of each species are. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Sana writes: "Saving one charismatic species, like the panda, saves the ecosystem." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Protecting panda habitat also protects many species (umbrella species), but whole ecosystems need wider management.
items.markingKey: Protecting panda habitat also protects many species (umbrella species), but whole ecosystems need wider management. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the concentration of carbon dioxide in a sealed bottle affects the temperature rise when it is illuminated by a lamp, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: position of thermometer (shaded).
items.answer: direct light on the probe gives false readings
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (position of thermometer (shaded)) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: direct light on the probe gives false readings. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: Diego is investigating how the distance downstream from a sewage outlet affects the biodiversity of freshwater invertebrates. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the distance from the sewage outlet increases, then the diversity index will increase, because organic pollution is diluted and broken down, so oxygen levels recover and more sensitive species can survive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the distance from the sewage outlet increases, then the diversity index will increase, because organic pollution is diluted and broken down, so oxygen levels recover and more sensitive species can survive.

items.stem:
Lukas used survey data to record the population of a rare butterfly in a nature reserve in years after grazing management began (three transects).

Years after management began | Butterflies counted per transect: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 24 | 24 | 24
2 | 36 | 38 | 38
4 | 69 | 71 | 73
6 | 94 | 97 | 62
8 | 108 | 105 | 107

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean butterflies counted per transect at 6, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 62 (trial 3 at 6); mean = 95.5
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (62) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 95.5.

items.stem: A forest of 60000 km² loses 5000 km² per year. Calculate the percentage lost after 8 years at this rate.

In an investigation into how the distance downstream from a sewage outlet affects the biodiversity of freshwater invertebrates, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: sampling time (1 min) and net size.
items.answer: longer sampling catches more
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (sampling time (1 min) and net size) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: longer sampling catches more. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: Ecologists caught and marked 30 fish in a pond and released them. A week later they caught 50 fish, of which 8 were marked. Estimate the population size (N = number marked × number in second sample ÷ number recaptured).
items.answer: 188 fish
items.markingKey: M1 30 × 50 ÷ 8; A1 188; (assumes marks not lost, no births/deaths/migration, random mixing).

items.stem: Briefly describe Minamata disease (Japan, 1950s) and explain what it reveals about bioaccumulation.
items.answer: A factory released mercury into Minamata Bay; it bioaccumulated in fish and shellfish and poisoned thousands of people who ate them. It led to the 2013 Minamata Convention to control mercury pollution worldwide.
items.markingKey: Context (A factory released mercury into Minamata Bay; it bioaccumulated in fish and shellfish and poisoned thousands of people who ate them.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It led to the 2013 Minamata Convention to control mercury pollution worldwide. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to bioaccumulation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Biodiversity should be protected mainly because of its value to humans (e.g. medicines, food)."
items.answer: Economic arguments help, but biodiversity is also worth protecting for its own sake and for unknown future value.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: provides medicines (e.g. aspirin from willow), food crops, pollination worth billions; easier to persuade governments. Arguments against: species have intrinsic value regardless of usefulness; we cannot predict which species will be useful. Supported judgement: Economic arguments help, but biodiversity is also worth protecting for its own sake and for unknown future value.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the mesh size of a fishing net affects the proportion of juvenile fish caught, using a model with different-sized beads. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): mop up water spills; small beads are a choking hazard. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. mop up water spills; small beads are a choking hazard); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: "Individual actions, such as eating less meat, can make a real difference to climate change." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Individual actions help and influence others, but large-scale policy change is essential.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: food is about a quarter of emissions; diets matter; collective action shifts markets. Arguments against: energy, industry and policy changes have far larger effects. Supported judgement: Individual actions help and influence others, but large-scale policy change is essential. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Yusuf investigated how the distance downstream from a sewage outlet affects the biodiversity of freshwater invertebrates. The method had this weakness: samples were taken in pools at some sites and riffles at others. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: sample the same type of microhabitat (riffles) at every site
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: sample the same type of microhabitat (riffles) at every site
